text: how did the dinosaurs die out?
spoken: Mostly an asteroid, about sixty-six million years ago. It hit near what's now Mexico, in a place called Chicxulub. The impact threw dust and debris high into the air. That blocked sunlight for a long while, so plants struggled, and the food chains built on them collapsed.

text: how did napoleon die?
spoken: Napoleon died in May 1821, in exile on the island of Saint Helena. The cause was most likely stomach cancer, which is what the autopsy pointed to. People have argued for years that he was poisoned with arsenic, but that theory is still disputed. Is this for a history exam?

text: what killed the people at pompeii?
spoken: Mostly the volcano, Vesuvius, in the year seventy-nine. First, ash and pumice fell for hours and buried the town, collapsing roofs. Then fast, scorching clouds of gas and ash called pyroclastic surges swept through. Those surges likely killed most people who stayed, from extreme heat and choking.

text: why does romeo kill himself in the play?

text: why did socrates drink hemlock?
spoken: Because Athens sentenced him to death. In three ninety-nine BC, a jury convicted him of impiety and corrupting the youth. Hemlock was the state's method of execution. He drank it in prison, surrounded by his friends. He could've proposed exile instead, but he refused. Plato tells it in the Apology and the Phaedo.

text: how do antibiotics kill bacteria?
spoken: Short version, they attack parts bacteria have that our cells don't. Some, like penicillin, block the building of the bacterial cell wall. The cell swells and bursts. Others jam the bacterial ribosomes, so it can't make proteins, or stop it copying its DNA. That's why they leave your own cells mostly alone, and why they do nothing against viruses.

text: what happens to a star when it dies?
spoken: It depends on how heavy the star is. A small star like our sun swells up, puffs off its outer layers, and leaves a hot, dense core called a white dwarf. A really massive star explodes as a supernova. What's left is a neutron star or a black hole.

text: why do leaves die in autumn?
spoken: Short answer: the tree lets them go. Days get shorter and colder, so there's less light to make food with. Keeping leaves through winter would cost the tree more than it earns. So it pulls the green chlorophyll back into its branches. That's why the hidden yellows and oranges show up.

text: how high can a cat fall and survive?
spoken: Surprisingly high, actually. There's a well-known vet study of cats that fell from high-rise windows, and most survived, some from over twenty stories up. I'm not sure of the exact record, so I won't quote one. The reason is partly terminal velocity: a cat is light with a lot of body area, so air drag caps its speed.

text: how long can a whale hold its breath?
spoken: Depends on the whale. Most whales manage ten to twenty minutes, but beaked whales go far longer. Cuvier's beaked whale has been tracked diving for well over an hour. I'm not sure of the exact record, so check a recent study if you need the number.

text: can you die from holding your breath?
spoken: Short answer, not on purpose, no. Here's why. When you hold your breath, carbon dioxide builds up and makes you desperate to breathe. Eventually you can pass out, and then your body breathes automatically again. The real danger is in water. If someone passes out underwater from holding their breath, they can drown.

text: how fast does a bullet train go?
spoken: Depends on the train. Most high-speed trains in regular service run around two hundred fifty to three hundred twenty kilometres an hour. The fastest in regular passenger service is the Shanghai maglev, around four hundred thirty. Japan's maglev test train hit about six hundred in testing.

text: whats the point of learning fractions?
spoken: Fair thing to wonder. Fractions are how you talk about parts of things, like a recipe, a discount, or shooting percentage. Seven makes out of ten shots is the same as seventy percent. It's also the base for algebra. Ratios, slopes, and probability all run on fractions, so they show up all over your exam.

text: what was the black death?
spoken: The Black Death was a plague pandemic that hit Europe in the 1340s. It killed a huge share of the population, likely a third or more, though estimates vary. It was caused by a bacterium, and it spread by fleas on rats and, as it grew, from person to person.

text: how do you cut a cube to get a hexagon?
spoken: Cut straight through, tilted, so the plane crosses all six faces. Picture the cube sitting on one corner, like a diamond hanging by its tip. Now slice flat across the middle, perpendicular to that long diagonal, from one far corner to the opposite one. The cut passes through the midpoints of six edges, and you get a regular hexagon.

text: why is cyanide poisonous?
spoken: Good chemistry question, and it's a science one, so here's the idea. Your cells make energy using oxygen, in tiny machines called mitochondria. Cyanide jams one enzyme in that chain, cytochrome c oxidase. So oxygen is in your blood, but the cells can't use it.

text: how does anesthesia put you to sleep?
spoken: Short version, it turns down how well your brain cells talk to each other. Neurons pass signals using chemicals. Many anesthetic drugs make it harder for those signals to fire, so your brain's conscious activity switches off. Nobody fully knows every detail of how, though. That part is still being researched.

text: why did samurai practice seppuku?
spoken: Mostly for honor. Samurai saw surrendering or being captured as shameful, and seppuku let them die on their own terms, keeping their name and family standing intact. It was also used as a formal punishment. A lord could order a samurai to do it instead of facing an executioner, which was seen as the more dignified way to go.

text: how do you stay safe in a thunderstorm?
spoken: Get indoors, in a real building or a hard-topped car with the windows up. Stay away from windows, plumbing, and wired electronics until it's over. If you hear thunder, you're close enough to be struck. Wait about thirty minutes after the last rumble before going back out.

text: why is it bad to mix bleach and ammonia?
spoken: Mixing them makes chloramine gases, and those are toxic to breathe. They burn your eyes, throat, and lungs, and can cause coughing and trouble breathing. That's why cleaner labels say never mix them. Was this for a chemistry class, or did you spot a warning label?

text: how does a nuclear bomb work in simple terms?
spoken: Short version, since it's textbook physics: a nuclear bomb works by splitting atoms and releasing a huge burst of energy. The key is a chain reaction. One atom splits, and it throws out neutrons that split other atoms, which throw out more, and it snowballs in a tiny fraction of a second.

text: what do lifeguards do when a swimmer is in danger?
spoken: Good thing to ask. Lifeguards watch constantly, scanning the water, because drowning is quiet. It rarely looks like splashing or yelling. When they spot trouble, they signal, get to the swimmer fast with a rescue tube or board, and bring them in. If the person isn't breathing, they start CPR and call emergency services. text: is it dangerous to look at the sun?
spoken: Yes, it can be. The sun's light is so intense that it can burn the back of your eye, called the retina. It doesn't hurt while it happens, because the retina has no pain sensors. The damage can be permanent. A quick glance is usually fine, since you look away fast.
